newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Democracy crisis overshadows OAU "economic summit".
newsitem.headline: Democracy crisis overshadows OAU "economic summit".

text.p: Turmoil in Sierra Leone after soldiers seized power from an elected government and problems in securing democracy in Africa looked set to dominate a summit of the Organisation of African Unity opening in Zimbabwe on Monday.

The three-day meeting, called to focus on ecomonic issues, has attracted nearly 30 heads of state or government, including Laurent Kabila of the Democratic Republic of Congo who ousted veteran Zairean president Mobutu Sese Seko last month.
Some African diplomats said they feared the OAU might be trying to concentrate on economic development in an effort to duck the tough political challenges facing the continent.

The runup to the summit was overshadowed by the military coup in the West African state of Sierra Leone and by Kabila's seven-month guerrilla campaign against Mobutu, who was one of the world's longest serving presidents.

OAU officials said Sierra Leone's case demonstrated a need to respect democratic institutions, while Kabila's renamed Democratic Republic of Congo showed a need for leaders to establish democratic rule to help to avert civil wars.
"These issues and all the other difficult problems will be looked at during the summit," said Ibrahim Dagash, spokesman for the OAU secretariat.

But a diplomatic source said a two-day OAU foreign ministers' conference ending on Friday had hardly debated "the hard facts" of former Zaire or of Sierra Leone, where junior army officers ousted democratically-elected President Ahmad Tejan Kabbah a week ago.
The foreign ministers instead made strenuous efforts to avoid discord, diplomats said, and did not go beyond simply calling for an end to the coup in Sierra Leone and congratulating Kabila.
Real debate on the the sovereignty of African states must include the possible precedent created by alleged support from neighbouring countries for Kabila's war to oust Mobutu, the diplomats said.

Rwanda, Burundi, Uganda and Angola are among states denying allegations that they gave military help to Kabila's whirlwind campaign to end Mobutu's 32-year-old regime, regarded as one of the world's most corrupt dictatorships.

The 53-member OAU says it wants the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) to help to restore constitutional rule in Sierra Leone, but Zimbabwean Foreign Minister Stan Mudenge said the mechanisms of how to do this were not discussed.
Such a discussion, some delegates said, would plunge the OAU into a debate on the morality of ECOWAS, which is dominated by military-ruled Nigeria, in leading others towards democracy.
OAU Secretary-General Salim Ahmed Salim said the summit must place emphasis on how Africa could realise its quest for an economic community by 2030.
